L0@P0: FloMo: Tractable Motion Prediction with Normalizing Flows
L1@P0: Christoph Scholler ¨
L2@P0: 1
L3@P0: and Alois Knoll2
L4@P0: Abstract— The future motion of traffic participants is inherently uncertain. To plan safely, therefore, an autonomous agent
L5@P0: must take into account multiple possible trajectory outcomes
L6@P0: and prioritize them. Recently, this problem has been addressed
L7@P0: with generative neural networks. However, most generative
L8@P0: models either do not learn the true underlying trajectory distribution reliably, or do not allow predictions to be associated with
L9@P0: likelihoods. In our work, we model motion prediction directly as
L10@P0: a density estimation problem with a normalizing flow between
L11@P0: a noise distribution and the future motion distribution. Our
L12@P0: model, named FloMo, allows likelihoods to be computed in a
L13@P0: single network pass and can be trained directly with maximum
L14@P0: likelihood estimation. Furthermore, we propose a method to
L15@P0: stabilize training flows on trajectory datasets and a new data
L16@P0: augmentation transformation that improves the performance
L17@P0: and generalization of our model. Our method achieves stateof-the-art performance on three popular prediction datasets,
L18@P0: with a significant gap to most competing models.
L19@P0: I. INTRODUCTION
L20@P0: For autonomous agents like vehicles and robots, it is
L21@P0: essential to accurately predict the movement of other agents
L22@P0: in their vicinity. Only with this ability collisions can be
L23@P0: avoided and interactions become safe. However, trajectories
L24@P0: can never be predicted with absolute certainty and multiple
L25@P0: future outcomes must be taken into account.
L26@P0: To address this problem, research on generative models
L27@P0: for motion prediction has recently gained attention. An ideal
L28@P0: generative model is expressive and able to learn the true
L29@P0: underlying trajectory distribution. Furthermore, it allows the
L30@P0: assignment of a likelihood value to each prediction. The
L31@P0: knowledge of how likely certain trajectories are is important
L32@P0: to prioritize, because it is infeasible for an agent to take into
L33@P0: account all possible future behaviors of surrounding agents.
L34@P0: Yet, most methods do not have all of these desirable
L35@P0: properties. For example, Generative Adversarial Networks
L36@P0: (GANs) have been used extensively for motion prediction [1], [2], [3], but suffer from mode collapse and are
L37@P0: not guaranteed to learn the true distribution of the data [4],
L38@P0: [5]. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are a popular type of
L39@P0: generative models as well [6], [7], [8], [9] and approximate
L40@P0: the true distribution with a lower bound. Unfortunately,
L41@P0: likelihoods cannot be calculated directly with VAEs and
L42@P0: must be estimated with computationally expensive Monte
L43@P0: Carlo methods. Other contributions try to overcome the
L44@P0: problem of missing likelihoods with the use of parametric
L45@P0: density functions, most commonly normal distributions [10],

L47@P0: State of Bavaria, Munich, Germany

L49@P0: Germany

L51@P0: likely trajectories are drawn more opaque. The distributions
L52@P0: our model learned are highly multi-modal.
L53@P0: [11]. However, this often requires unrealistic independence
L54@P0: assumptions and provides only limited expressive power.
L55@P0: In this work, we propose a novel motion prediction
L56@P0: model that addresses the aforementioned issues. In particular,
L57@P0: our model FloMo is based on normalizing flows that we
L58@P0: condition on observed motion histories. It is expressive and
L59@P0: able to learn complex multi-modal distributions over future
L60@P0: trajectories (see Fig. 1). With FloMo, trajectories can be
L61@P0: efficiently sampled and likelihoods are computed in closed
L62@P0: form. These tractable likelihoods allow us to train our model
L63@P0: with maximum likelihood estimation, instead of a proxy
L64@P0: loss. Because, as we show, trajectory data is prone to cause
L65@P0: divergence of likelihoods during training, we apply a novel
L66@P0: noise injection method that significantly stabilizes training
L67@P0: and enables the use of our model’s likelihoods in downstream
L68@P0: tasks. Furthermore, we propose a new data augmentation
L69@P0: transformation that helps our model to generalize better and
L70@P0: improves its performance. We demonstrate with an extensive
L71@P0: evaluation on three popular motion prediction datasets that
L72@P0: our method achieves state-of-the-art performance and we
L73@P0: show, both qualitatively and quantitatively, that the likelihoods our model produces are meaningful.
L74@P0: II. RELATED WORK
L75@P0: Many classic approaches have been developed to make
L76@P0: trajectory predictions [12], [13], [14], and are still relevant
L77@P0: today [15].
L78@P0: Neural Networks. However, after successes on various other computer vision problems, neural networks have
L79@P0: become popular for motion prediction as well. Alahi et
L80@P0: al. [16] use Long Short-Term Memories (LSTMs) to predict
L81@P0-1: arXiv:2103.03614v2 [cs.CV] 30 Jul 2021pedestrian trajectories and share information between agents
L82@P1: with a social hidden state pooling. Similarly, Pfeiffer et
L83@P1: al. [17] provide an LSTM with an occupancy grid of static
L84@P1: objects and an angular grid of surrounding pedestrians. But
L85@P1: also Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [18], spatiotemporal graphs [19] or state refinement modules [20] have
L86@P1: been proposed to predict single trajectories.
L87@P1: Generative Models. To predict not only a single trajectory, but multiple possible outcomes, prediction methods
L88@P1: based on generative neural networks have been developed.
L89@P1: Sadeghian et al. [2] as well as Gupta et al. [1] utilize GANs
L90@P1: that are provided with additional context information. To
L91@P1: fight mode collapse, Amirian et al. [3] use an Info-GAN
L92@P1: with an attention pooling module. The Trajectron++ model
L93@P1: of Salzmann et al. [21] combines a conditional VAE, LSTMs
L94@P1: and spatio-temporal graphs to produce multi-modal trajectory
L95@P1: predictions. Inspired by BERT, Giuliari et al. [22] propose
L96@P1: to use a transformer architecture for motion prediction. Xue
L97@P1: et al. [9] propose the Scene Gated Social Graph that models
L98@P1: the relations between pedestrians with a dynamic graph that
L99@P1: is used to condition a VAE. Mohamed et al. [23] model
L100@P1: social interactions with a spatio-temporal graph on which
L101@P1: they apply graph convolutions and a temporal CNN to
L102@P1: make predictions. Instead of directly predicting trajectories,
L103@P1: Mangalam et al. [24] use a conditional VAE to first predict
L104@P1: trajectory endpoints and a recursive social pooling module
L105@P1: to make trajectory predictions. The prediction model of
L106@P1: Pajouheshgar et al. [25] is fully convolutional and outputs
L107@P1: a discrete probability distribution over image pixels.
L108@P1: Normalizing Flows. While originally developed for density estimation [26], normalizing flows have recently been
L109@P1: applied to various data generation problems [27], [28]. In the
L110@P1: area of motion prediction, normalizing flows have been rarely
L111@P1: used. To generate trajectories for a planner, Agarwal et al. [7]
L112@P1: sample from a conditional β-VAE [29] that uses a Neural Autoregressive Flow [30] as a flexible posterior. Bhattacharyya
L113@P1: et al. [8] use a conditional Flow VAE with condition and
L114@P1: posterior regularization to predict trajectories. In their recently published work [31], they use a Block Autoregressive
L115@P1: Flow based on Haar wavelets to learn distributions for motion
L116@P1: prediction and also adapted FlowWaveNet [27] for motion
L117@P1: prediction. Ma et al. [32] recently showed how to find those
L118@P1: trajectories sampled from affine flows that are both likely
L119@P1: and diverse to make predictions.
L120@P1: The method we propose in this work is a flow-based
L121@P1: generative model that can learn complex multimodal distributions. It allows tractable likelihood computation and
L122@P1: can be trained directly with maximum likelihood estimation.
L123@P1: Most existing generative models only possess some of these
L124@P1: properties. In contrast to the flow-based prediction models
L125@P1: proposed in concurrent works [31], [32], the flow we use
L126@P1: is based on splines and hence is more flexible, which our
L127@P1: results demonstrate. Furthermore, we propose a novel noise
L128@P1: injection method that significantly stabilizes training and a
L129@P1: data augmentation transformation that further improves our
L130@P1: model’s generalization and performance. In our extensive
L131@P1: experiments we show that our model achieves state-of-theart results on popular motion prediction datasets and that the
L132@P1: likelihoods it produces are meaningful and can be used to
L133@P1: modulate how concentrated our model’s predictions are.

L187@P1: IV. METHOD
L188@P1: The objective of our model is to learn the conditional
L189@P1: motion distribution p(x | o), where o is an observed trajectory and x is the trajectory to predict (see Sec. III).
L190@P1: We learn this distribution by utilizing normalizing flows. To
L191@P1: then make a prediction, we sample from a standard normal
L192@P1: base distribution u ∼ N (µ= 0, σ= 1) and pass the sample
L193@P1: through our model, which we condition with the encoded
L194@P1: observed trajectory o. The output of our model is a sampled
L195@P1: trajectory prediction xˆ. By evaluating Eq. 2, we can directly
L196@P1: compute the likelihood of each sample in the same network
L197@P1: pass. An overview of our architecture is given in Fig. 2.
L198@P1: The main components of our model are a motion encoder
L199@P1: and neural spline flows as proposed by Durkan et al. [34],
L200@P1: consisting of conditional coupling layers [35] and monotonic
L201@P1: spline transformations [36].
L202@P1: In this work we focus on the prediction of individual
L203@P1-2: agents, because tests with integrating common interactionFig. 2: Our model is composed of multiple flow modules, each containing a coupling layer for conditioning, a monotonic

L206@P2: modules in our model’s conditioning did not lead to relevant
L207@P2: performance improvements. This is in line with the findings
L208@P2: in [15], [1] and [22]. In the following sections, we explain
L209@P2: each component of our model in detail, including how we
L210@P2: prepare our data to achieve stable training, our objective

L213@P2: A. Motion Encoder
L214@P2: The first module of our model is the motion encoder,
L215@P2: which encodes the observed trajectory o. Before we encode
L216@P2: o, we subtract from each position p
L217@P2: t ∈ o its preceding
L218@P2: position, i.e. p
L219@P2: 0t = pt − pt−1
L220@P2: . This means instead of encoding absolute coordinates, we encode relative displacements,
L221@P2: which has proven to be beneficial for motion prediction [37],
L222@P2: [15]. From now on, we will denote the resulting relative observed trajectory as o
L223@P2: 0
L224@P2: and its encoding as c. We implement
L225@P2: the encoder as a recurrent neural network with three Gated
L226@P2: Recurrent Units (GRUs) [38] and a hidden state size of 16.
L227@P2: Before we pass each displacement step to the encoder, we
L228@P2: embed it with a linear layer in a 16 dimensional vector. The
L229@P2: output of the last GRU is then passed through an Exponential
L230@P2: Linear Unit (ELU) [39] and again linearly transformed, while
L231@P2: keeping 16 output dimensions. We determined these hidden
L232@P2: and embedding sizes empirically. Because the ELU function
L233@P2: is non-zero everywhere, it helps to avoid dying neurons in the
L234@P2: network recursion. The recurrent architecture of our encoder
L235@P2: enables it to work with input trajectories of various lengths.
L236@P2: B. Conditional Coupling Layer
L237@P2: One way to design a normalizing flow is to modularize it
L238@P2: into a transformation and a conditioner [30]. The conditioner
L239@P2: takes the input u and parameterizes the transformation that
L240@P2: in turn transforms u into x. In our work, it is important
L241@P2: that our flow is fast to evaluate both in the forward and
L242@P2: inverse direction. For sampling trajectories, we must transform forward from u to x, but during training we have to
L243@P2: compute the likelihood of x in the inverse direction (Eq. 3).
L244@P2: Furthermore, it would be desirable for our model to allow
L245@P2: the computation of likelihoods for trajectories that an agent
L246@P2: could possibly take, but that were not sampled. This also
L247@P2: requires the inverse direction.
L248@P2: For the flow to be fast to invert, both the transformation
L249@P2: and conditioner must be fast to invert. To achieve this for the
L250@P2: conditioner, we use coupling layers [35], [34] to implement
L251@P2: our flow. Coupling layers are just as fast to invert, as they
L252@P2: are to compute forward. Our coupling layer computes the
L253@P2: output x as follows (⊕ denotes concatenation):
L254@P2: x1:d−1 = u1:d−1

L258@P2: First, we split the input u in half and assign the first part
L259@P2: u1:d−1 directly to the output. Then we concatenate u1:d−1
L260@P2: with trajectory encoding c (see Sec. IV-A) and feed it to
L261@P2: the conditioner network that computes the parameters θ.
L262@P2: Using θ to parameterize the invertible transformation τ ,
L263@P2: we transform the second half ud:n of u element-wise to
L264@P2: the remaining corresponding outputs. The resulting Jacobian
L265@P2: matrix is lower triangular, and hence its determinant can be
L266@P2: easily computed as the product of its diagonal elements [35].
L267@P2: By concatenating c to the conditioner input, we make our
L268@P2: flow conditional on the observed trajectory, such that it learns
L269@P2: the density p(x | o).
L270@P2: We implement the conditioner as a regular feed forward
L271@P2: neural network with five hidden layers. Each layer has
L272@P2: 32 neurons and is followed by an ELU activation. This
L273@P2: configuration worked well empirically. Because half of the
L274@P2: inputs are not transformed in a coupling layer, it is crucial to
L275@P2: stack several such modules and randomly permute the input
L276@P2: vectors between the modules. As permutations are volumepreserving, the Jacobian determinant of such a permutation
L277@P2: layer is simply 1.
L278@P2: C. Monotonic Spline Transforms
L279@P2: Transformations used in normalizing flows must be expressive, invertible and differentiable. In motion prediction,
L280@P2-3: expressive power is crucial to represent complex distributions and only fast invertibility allows the computationof likelihoods for query trajectories at runtime and short
L281@P3: training times. However, most expressive flows, e.g. neural
L282@P3: flows [30], cannot be inverted analytically and we have to
L283@P3: resort to iterative methods like bisection search [33]. On the
L284@P3: other hand, flows that are fast to invert often use simple
L285@P3: transformations, e.g. affine or linear transformations, and
L286@P3: hence are not very expressive.
L287@P3: However, recently Durkan et al. [34] proposed using
L288@P3: monotonic rational-quadratic splines (RQS) [36] as flow
L289@P3: transformations. In conjunction with coupling layers, this
L290@P3: kind of flow becomes both expressive and fast to invert. The
L291@P3: spline transformation described in the following corresponds
L292@P3: to the function τ in Sec. IV-B.

L433@P3: D. Preventing Manifolds
L434@P3: Whenever data is distributed such that it – or a subset of
L435@P3: it – is residing on a lower-dimensional manifold, this leads to
L436@P3: infinite likelihood spikes in the estimated density. Consider
L437@P3: the two-dimensional example with joint density p(x, y),
L438@P3: where x is normally distributed and y = x. The distribution
L439@P3: resides on a line and for R R p(y | x)p(x)dydx = 1 to hold,
L440@P3: the likelihoods where y is defined must be infinite.
L441@P3: In practice, this problem also arises when certain dimensions in the dataset samples frequently take on equal
L442@P3: values, or when one dimension frequently takes the same
L443@P3: value. Because we predict relative displacements x
L444@P3: 0
L445@P3: instead
L446@P3: of absolute coordinates, this can happen if pedestrians stand
L447@P3: still (values become zero), or if they move with constant
L448@P3: velocity for multiple timesteps (values are equal). During
L449@P3: training this can cause numerical instabilities, loss volatility
L450@P3: and the overestimation of certain samples’ likelihoods.
